extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy / economic history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how the real value of precious metals (especially silver) has varied historically and how to interpret historical price data; explains causes and proper measures for comparing monetary and commodity values. Useful for economic history, price-index interpretation, and classical value theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour is the real measure of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour, and not any particular commodity or set of commodities, is the real measure of the value both of silver and of all other commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quantity of labour that a commodity represents as the ultimate standard for comparing values; avoid inferring the real value of money from single commodity prices without referencing labour. (Text emphasizes labour as the 'ultimate price' and anchor for comparisons across societies and times.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corn (staple subsistence) is the most accurate commodity measure of silver's value
rubrics_metrics.description: Corn, or whatever is the common vegetable food of the people, is a more accurate measure of value than any other commodity or set of commodities for judging the real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer comparing silver to corn when estimating the real value of money because: (a) corn is produced by human industry (unlike many animal products), (b) average produce is closely matched to average consumption, and (c) raising equal quantities of corn tends to require nearly equal labour across stages of improvement. The money price of labour depends more on the price of subsistence (corn) than on prices of other rude produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three possible supply/demand combinations determine silver's value trajectory
rubrics_metrics.description: If demand increases while supply does not increase as much, silver's value rises; if supply increases faster than demand, silver becomes cheaper; if supply and demand increase nearly proportionally, silver's purchasing power remains nearly the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing historical price trends, classify periods according to these three dynamics (demand> supply, supply> demand, supply≈demand) to explain rising, falling, or stable money prices of corn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish increases in metal quantity by cause (mines vs. wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase in the quantity of precious metals from more abundant mines necessarily diminishes their value; an increase resulting from the greater wealth/annual produce of a country need not diminish the metals' value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting changes in money prices, identify whether coin abundance arose from new mining discoveries (supply shock lowering value) or from increased demand due to economic growth (which may maintain or raise metal value because more coin is needed to circulate greater production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion price (payments in kind) can mislead historical price measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Rents and payments often recorded as a fixed money sum in lieu of payments in kind (conversion price) tend to be set below market price and thus misrepresent ordinary market prices of commodities like corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat recorded 'conversion prices' as actual market prices; historical sources that mix in-kind and money conversions (e.g., Scottish conversion price) can understate ordinary prices. Fleetwood’s mistakes are given as an example where conversion prices were mistaken for market prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware transcription and copying errors in statutory/archival price records
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ancient statutes of assize and manuscript copies were transcribed incompletely or carelessly (often listing only the lowest price examples), misleading later interpreters about ordinary price levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check original manuscripts or fuller sources; be cautious when later editions omit higher-price clauses and when authors draw conclusions from incomplete transcriptions (e.g., assize of bread and ale transcriptions missing higher prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme low or high recorded prices can distort perception of ordinary prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Very low prices recorded for particular years (often due to local plenty) or very high prices (due to famine/war) should not be taken as indicators of ordinary prices; turbulent societies show greater variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical price series, average over appropriate periods and be wary of anecdotal extremes. Fleetwood’s collected prices often reflect extraordinary years and thus require cautious interpretation (use averages over multi-year divisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional transportation and market structure affect commodity prices independently of metal value
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in the money price of corn between towns and remote areas, and between countries (e.g., Holland, Genoa vs. interior), often reflect costs of transport and dependence on imports rather than differences in the real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute price differentials to carriage, freight, insurance, and local scarcity; do not infer a higher real value of silver in regions where important staples are dear because transport costs raise commodity prices more than they affect metal costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased national wealth raises demand for coin and plate, affecting metal prices
rubrics_metrics.description: As the annual produce of labour increases, a greater quantity of coin is necessary to circulate it and richer people demand more plate and ornaments; this increased demand tends to raise the price of gold and silver rather than lower it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret rising metal prices in growing economies as potentially demand-driven (greater need for coin and luxury use) rather than as evidence of diminishing metal value due to abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prices vary more in disorderly societies due to interrupted commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: In turbulent, disorderly societies where commerce and communication are interrupted, local scarcities and famines produce much larger swings in commodity prices than in more settled societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider political stability and market integration when comparing historical price volatility; under stronger central authority and security (e.g., Tudor England) price variability and extremes decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low money prices of unmanufactured commodities can reflect low real value of those goods, not high silver value
rubrics_metrics.description: Very low nominal prices for cattle, poultry, game, etc., in sparsely inhabited or uncultivated countries often indicate that these goods require little labour to acquire there; they do not imply silver has a high real value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concluding metal is especially valuable in regions with low money prices for spontaneous natural products; instead assess the labour embodied in those commodities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-year averages and aggregated divisions to infer ordinary prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-year prices are often misleading; Fleetwood’s compilation is organized into seven divisions of twelve years with averages at the end of each division to show trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing historical price trends, aggregate into multi-year blocks and compute averages to smooth out anomalous years and better detect long-run tendencies (e.g., decline then rise in silver value across centuries).
